segments.line: Here's the problem nobody warned you about.
Charging. Your charger needs a socket in the wall.
Mo's building has electric lights, but no sockets.
And lots of homes don't even have lights.
Even in 1940, the census found that more than one in five American homes had no electric lights at all. That's real.
You finally find a socket in a hotel lobby. You plug in.
Nothing.
Parts of New York still run on direct current, the old kind of electricity. Your charger was built for the other kind.
You lose a whole day, and twelve percent, hunting for the right socket.
In the end you pay a hotel porter a whole dollar to let you sit behind the front desk, next to the only socket that works,
while the guests stare at the glowing brick on the counter.
Then there's the bigger problem. Look at what you're holding.
The chip inside a recent iPhone can do thirty-five trillion operations every second.
The most famous computer of the next twenty years, ENIAC, won't be switched on until 1946.
It will weigh twenty-seven tonnes, fill a whole room, burn a hundred and fifty kilowatts of power, and
do five thousand additions a second. That's real too.
You're carrying a machine the world won't be able to build for half a century. And you've been showing it off in jazz clubs.
The newspapers stop calling it a lightning box. Now they just call it the device.
In January 1927, people will pay seventy-five dollars to talk to London for three minutes.
That's well over a thousand dollars in today's money. That's real.
So imagine what someone would pay for the thing in your pocket.
Forty-one percent.
